newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Third election chances fade for Argentina's Menem.
newsitem.headline: Third election chances fade for Argentina's Menem.

text.p: A bill widely seen as an attempt to pave the way for a third bid by Carlos Menem for Argentina's presidency looked doomed Friday after prominent members of his Peronist Party declared their opposition.

"It is politically inconvenient, it does not respond to the real needs of the Argentine people and not even Menem himself wants it," the Clarin newspaper quoted Peronist Congressman Pascual Rampi as saying.

Rampi is a supporter of Buenos Aires Governor Eduardo Duhalde, front-running Peronist candidate for presidential elections due in 1999. A third of Peronist congressmen are Duhalde supporters and they have the numbers to stop the bill.
Menem, 66, has repeatedly denied he would seek a third term but "Menem 99" banners have appeared at campaign functions in recent months.

Rumours of a move by Menem to change the constitution to allow himself a third term hit fever pitch when a close ally, Senator Jorge Yoma, introduced a bill earlier this week to allow referendums to be called to change the constitution.
Yoma has been evasive on the bill's purpose, but opposition parties were quick to accuse Menem of plotting a third term.

"If Carlos Menem keeps on with his imperial delusions of being reelected, he is going to follow in the footsteps of Bucaram," said Radical Party senator Raul Galvan, referring to Ecuador's former President Abdala Bucaram, who was dismissed by Congress last week.
Former Radical President Raul Alfonsin declared that those who supported Yoma's bill would be "infamous traitors to their country."
Alfonsin was instrumental in allowing Menem to make an earlier constitional modification in 1993, which allowed him to run for reelection in 1994.
Duhalde's supporters have made it clear they will kill the bill. The Buenos Aires governor has already postponed his presidential hopes once, in 1994, they said.
"Duhalde stepped down once before to allow a new Menem term, but that won't happen again," an unnamed Duhalde supporter told Clarin.
